prompt: Some governments now fund university places only in subjects that lead directly to employment. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Higher education is expensive, and the money that pays for it has to come from somewhere, so it is not unreasonable for a government to ask what its subsidy buys. My objection is not to the question but to the answer most funding formulas give, which treats a graduate's first salary as though it settled the matter.

Where a shortage is real and documented, targeted funding is straightforward good policy. A health service short of radiographers cannot conjure them out of a general commitment to learning; it needs places, in named programmes, paid for now against a need that will bite in five years. Steering money towards those places is not an attack on scholarship but the ordinary business of planning, and the alternative — subsidising every application equally and hoping the aggregate comes out right — has left some fields with graduate surpluses and others with chronic vacancies.

The trouble begins when employability stops being one input among several and becomes the only one. Earnings measured three years after graduation describe the labour market of the year a particular cohort happened to leave university, and they describe it only for the jobs that existed then. They cannot register the teacher a philosophy graduate becomes at forty, and they could not have anticipated that several of today's safest industries would be built on research that looked unusable a generation ago. Nor do they price what a country forfeits when the last people able to read its own archives are hobbyists.

So I would keep the shortage-driven funding and abandon the salary league tables that increasingly accompany it. Direct money where the evidence of need is specific; protect a floor beneath the disciplines whose payoff is diffuse and slow; and accept that some of what a university produces will never appear on a return-on-investment statement — which is an argument for funding it publicly, not an argument against funding it at all.
title: Funding only the degrees that lead to jobs
